extraction.name: COMMONSENSE QA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge
extraction.description: When answering a question, people often draw upon their rich world knowledge in addition to the particular context. Recent work has focused primarily on answering questions given some relevant document or context, and required very little general background. To investigate question answering with prior knowledge, we present COMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering. To capture common sense beyond associations, we extract from CONCEPTNET (Speer et al., 2017) multiple target concepts that have the same semantic relation to a single source concept. Crowd-workers are asked to author multiple-choice questions that mention the source concept and discriminate in tum between each of the target concepts. This encourages workers to create questions with complex semantics that often require prior knowledge. We create 12,247 questions through this procedure and demonstrate the difficulty of our task with a large number of strong baselines. Our best baseline is based on BERT-large (Devlin et al., 2018) and obtains 56% accuracy, well below human performance, which is 89%.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.publisher: School of Computer Science, Tel-Aviv University; Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process involves three main steps: 1. Extracting subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts. 2. Crowdsourcing workers to author three multiple-choice questions per subgraph (one per target concept), add two additional distractors per question, and verify questions’ quality. 3. Adding textual context to each question by querying a search engine and retrieving web snippets.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Subgraphs extracted from CONCEPTNET (Speer et al., 2017).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Before crowdsourcing, triplets from CONCEPTNET were filtered: 1. Triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or well-explored NLP relations (e.g., IsA) were removed, using 22 specific relations. 2. Triplets where concepts were more than four words or not in English were filtered. 3. Triplets where the edit distance between c1 and c2 was too low were filtered. This resulted in 236,208 triplets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were presented with a question concept and three answer concepts. They were instructed to formulate three questions, each containing the question concept and having one of the target concepts as the correct answer, while the other two were distractors. Workers were encouraged to avoid surface clues. For each formulated question, workers added two additional incorrect answers: one selected from CONCEPTNET concepts with the same relation to the question concept, and another manually formulated by the worker. Each question ultimately had one correct answer and four distractors. A disjoint group of workers verified the generated questions, annotating them as unanswerable or choosing the right answer. Each question was verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were retained, filtering out 15% of questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions were verified by a disjoint group of workers. Each question was verified by 2 workers. Only questions verified by at least one worker who answered correctly were used, filtering out 15% of the questions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning of Natural Language Understanding (NLU) systems, particularly for commonsense question answering.
